 - Do not move the target away after turning on the lamp.
 - Do not shuttle multiple same-type candidates between locations; remain at the lamp and finish with one co-located target.
 
+## Admissible Actions
+
+- Before committing to a navigation or manipulation command, verify that the command is present in the current admissible action list; if it is not, do not issue it.
+- When a desired navigation destination is absent but a direct action on that receptacle is listed, use the direct action if appropriate; otherwise choose a different admissible action that advances the search or task.
+
 ## General Non-Desklamp Retrieval, Cleaning, and Placement
 
 For ordinary put, clean, or transfer tasks where no desklamp is required, use this procedure instead.
 
-1. Identify and search for the exact requested target. If it is not visible, search systematically: open any closed cabinet, drawer, or fridge immediately upon reaching it and inspect its contents before leaving. Do not immediately revisit an already-open receptacle that visibly lacks the target; choose a different uninspected candidate location instead. Do not repeatedly check inventory while carrying nothing. Continue until the exact target is found or all plausible candidate receptacles have been inspected once.
-2. Manipulate only the exact requested target category. Do not pick up, clean, or place a substitute object when the exact target is absent; for example, do not transfer a soapbottle when the task requests a dishsponge. If the exact target has not yet been found, continue the systematic search rather than completing the transfer with a non-target object.
+1. Identify and search for the exact requested target. If it is not visible, search systematically: open any closed cabinet, drawer, or fridge immediately upon reaching it and inspect its contents before leaving, and include visible open surfaces such as tables, countertops, shelves, and sidetables rather than only closed drawers or cabinets. If an opened receptacle visibly lacks the target, leave it and choose a different uninspected candidate from the current admissible list; do not re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle among the same few locations. After checking receptacles of one type, move to a still-unexamined receptacle, preferring a type you have not yet tried, before re-checking a location that the current or recent observations show was already opened or seen to lack the target. Do not repeatedly check inventory while carrying nothing. Continue until the exact target is found or all plausible candidate receptacles have been inspected once.
+2. Manipulate only the exact requested target category. When the task requests an exact object and that exact noun phrase has not been observed, do not acquire, clean, cool, heat, or place a different but related object as a substitute; for example, do not transfer a soapbottle when the task requests a dishsponge. If a container holds only a non-matching object, leave it without manipulating that object and continue searching for the exact target. Do not treat conditioning or placement of a non-target object as progress toward the task; only the exact requested object satisfies the goal. If the exact target has not yet been found, continue the systematic search rather than completing the transfer with a non-target object.
 3. Acquire the exact target. If the task requires the object to be clean, carry it to an appropriate cleaning receptacle such as a sinkbasin and perform the clean action. If no cleaning is requested, skip the cleaning detour.
 4. Go directly to the requested destination. Open it first if it is closed, then place or move the target there. Do not detour to unrelated receptacles or release the target before the requested placement is completed.

items.text: The current diff adds three things to the desklamp skill's general non-desklamp procedure—an 'Admissible Actions' verification clause, a broadened/anti-cycling search step, and a strengthened exact-target/no-substitute step—so its observed response is a joint intervention and cannot be credited to a single clause. Across the 10 verified pairs, task-level success was unchanged: both the pre-edit Parent and the edited Candidate succeeded on 8 tasks, and both hit the 50-step limit on the same two tasks (clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer; put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet). Step counts moved in both directions (Candidate 6 vs 5 in examine-the-pillow-with-the-desklamp and put-some-pencil-on-desk; 11 vs 14 in cool-some-apple-and-put-it-in-microwave), so no clause is isolated and no task-level improvement or regression is demonstrated in this single trial per task.

The newly added 'Admissible Actions' clause requires verifying that a navigation or manipulation command is present in the current admissible list before issuing it, and using a listed direct action on a receptacle when the desired navigation destination is absent. In the observed runs this was not reliably followed: the Candidate still issued navigation commands absent from the admissible list—'go to cabinet 3' from cabinet 1 (Q8:39) and 'go to drawer 8' from drawer 7 (Q7:25)—each returning 'Nothing happens', and the Parent likewise issued an inadmissible 'go to cabinet 1' from cabinet 3 (P8:15). No observed step shows the intended direct-action fallback producing progress, and both put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet runs still ended at the 50-step limit (P8:50, Q8:50).

The revised search step directs the Actor to include visible open surfaces, to prefer a still-untried receptacle type after exhausting one type, and not to re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle. The observed response is mixed. Consistent with the clause, in the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair the Candidate visited receptacle types the Parent never reached—bathtubbasin 1 (Q8:3) and sinkbasin 2 (Q8:19)—yet the requested soapbar was not found and both sides still hit the step limit (P8:50, Q8:50). The clause did not break the cycling failure mode: in the clean-butterknife-in-drawer and soapbar-in-cabinet pairs both sides still shuttled among the same receptacles to the 50-step limit (P7:50, Q7:50). In two tasks where the target was found the Candidate spent an extra initial navigation step (Q2:1, Q5:1), giving 6 vs 5 steps, though that inefficiency is not individually isolated.

The revised step 2 states that when the exact requested noun has not been observed, a different but related object must not be acquired, cleaned, cooled, heated, or placed, and that a container holding only a non-matching object should be left unmanipulated. A counterexample appeared in the clean-some-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer task: no butterknife was observed, yet the Candidate took a knife from drawer 1 (Q7:9, Q7:13), cleaned it (Q7:17) and moved it to drawer 1 (Q7:19), i.e., it substituted a related object despite the strengthened rule, and the run still ended at the 50-step limit (Q7:50); the Parent substituted the same knife (P7:8, P7:12). In the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet task the exact soapbar was likewise absent and the Candidate left the visible near-miss soapbottle/spraybottle at cabinet 2 untaken (seen at Q8:7, never taken), but the Parent also abstained there, so that pair does not distinguish the clause.

Earlier no-substitute tightenings in this sequence (S1_R03 and S1_R04 diffs) were tested mainly when the exact target was absent: in a cool-a-pan pair the Parent eventually took a pot, cooled it, and moved it while the Candidate saw the same pot without manipulating it; in a heat-a-mug pair the Parent took and moved a cup while the Candidate left it; and in the later hot-mug pair the Parent took cup 2 and heated it while the Candidate left the visible cup untouched and kept searching empty-handed. Both sides still hit the 50-step limit in those tasks because the exact pan or mug was never found, so Candidate abstention avoided near-miss manipulation but did not create success. This supports only conditional value for the no-substitute rule—it can prevent ineffective substitute handling when the exact category is absent, but task success still depended on locating the exact target, and these observations did not isolate the rule from simultaneous temperature and search guidance.

The current diff pushes the no-substitute rule further in the general procedure, stating that when the exact requested noun phrase has not been observed the Actor must not acquire, clean, cool, heat, or place a different but related object, and that a container holding only a non-matching object should be left unmanipulated. This produced no consistent Candidate advantage in the two current target-absent tasks. In val:0007 (clean a butterknife into drawer) the butterknife was absent; both Parent and Candidate took and cleaned a knife—e.g., Candidate Q7:9 took knife 1, Q7:17 cleaned it, and Q7:19 moved it to drawer 1—so the Candidate itself violated the tightened rule and both reached the 50-step limit. In val:0008 (clean a soapbar into cabinet) the soapbar was absent and cabinet 2 held soapbottle 2; both Parent and Candidate left that soapbottle unmanipulated (P8:13, Q8:13–Q8:14) and both again reached the step limit. Thus the stronger wording was not associated with differential no-substitute behavior: it failed to stop a knife-for-butterknife substitution in one case and merely matched the Parent's abstention in the other. By contrast, in val:0006 where the exact butterknife was present, both sides acquired it, cleaned it at the sinkbasin, and placed it in the drawer, each succeeding in 8 steps, so the rule did not impede exact-target completion.

In the S1_R03 edit, the search step added anti-cycling and step-budget-priority language: use current/recent observations to avoid immediate cycling; do not re-examine an already-open empty receptacle or check inventory while carrying nothing; and when the obvious cabinets/fridge fail or the step count is high, prefer uninspected drawers, shelves, the diningtable, or new unopened containers over known-empty locations. The response was mixed. Positive: in a cool-a-bread pair the Parent shuttled among the fridge, cabinets and countertops to the 50-step limit without finding bread, while the Candidate went to the diningtable, took a bread there, cooled it at the fridge, and placed it on countertop 1 for a success. Negative: in a same-task pair with identical room and container contents, the Parent went to countertop 3 and took the bread there, whereas the Candidate repeatedly visited countertop 2, never went to countertop 3, cycled among cabinets, shelves and the fridge, and hit the step limit. In the cool-a-plate pair the Candidate chose an unavailable move to cabinet 3 (no-op), re-examined that empty location, reached the plate in cabinet 9 only at step 49, and exhausted the budget at 50, while the Parent succeeded at step 38 after finding the plate in cabinet 9. In the remaining cool-a-pan and heat-a-mug tasks both sides ended at the step limit while shuttling among the same cabinets, stoveburners and other receptacles. The visible S1_R03 pairs were mixed rather than a net Candidate improvement: Parent P2 and P6 succeeded where Candidate Q2 and Q6 hit the limit; Candidate Q4 succeeded where Parent P4 hit the limit; P7/Q7, P8/Q8, and P9/Q9 succeeded on both sides; and P5 and P10 and their Candidates all reached the step limit. Each task was run once and target locations varied, so this clause alone cannot be credited or blamed for the pattern.

The current diff rewrites the search step again: include visible open surfaces such as tables, countertops, shelves and sidetables rather than only closed drawers/cabinets; after checking receptacles of one type, prefer a still-unexamined receptacle type before re-checking a location already opened or seen to lack the target; and do not re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle. In the current pairs this was associated with some broader exploration—Candidate Q8 visited bathtubbasin (Q8:3) and sinkbasin 2 (Q8:19), locations absent from Parent P8's trace, and Candidate Q5 checked the desk (Q5:1) before going to drawer 1 (Q5:2), adding one step but preserving success. However, the two exact-target-absent tasks still failed identically: val:0007 (clean a butterknife into drawer) and val:0008 (clean a soapbar into cabinet) both ended at the 50-step limit in Parent and Candidate, and Q8 continued cycling among cabinets 1–4 (e.g., Q8:20, Q8:22, Q8:23, Q8:24, Q8:25, Q8:30). In straightforward pairs where the target was directly reachable—val:0001 (bowl with desklamp), val:0003 and val:0004 (mug to sidetable), and val:0006 (clean butterknife to drawer)—the Candidate also succeeded at the same step counts as the Parent (4, 4, 4, and 8 steps; Q1:4, Q3:4, Q4:4, Q6:8 vs P1:4, P3:4, P4:4, P6:8), so the rewritten search step did not degrade direct completion. Overall, the added search-breadth/prefer-new-type wording did not break the cycling failure mode when the exact target was missing, and open-surface checks can add steps without changing task success.

The current diff adds an Admissible Actions section requiring the Actor to verify a navigation/manipulation command is present in the current admissible list before issuing it, and, when a desired navigation destination is absent but a direct action on that receptacle is listed, to use that direct action or otherwise choose a different admissible action. Across the 10 current pairs the clause had limited observable effect because almost every executed action was admissible. The clearest genuine absent-menu attempts occurred in the val:0008 clean-soapbar task: Parent issued 'go to cabinet 1' at P8:15 (feedback action_in_admissible_commands=false), got 'Nothing happens', and then used the admissible 'examine cabinet 1' at P8:16; Candidate issued 'go to cabinet 3' at Q8:39 (also false), got 'Nothing happens', and then used the admissible 'examine cabinet 3' at Q8:40. Thus the Candidate still issued a command absent from its menu despite the new verification clause, and its fallback mirrored the Parent's behavior rather than demonstrating an added benefit. Both executions remained in the same step-limit soapbar search (P8:50, Q8:50), so no task-level improvement can be attributed to this section.

The remaining non-admissible actions in the current batch were output-formatting failures rather than menu-absence: Parent P8:12 was an empty action and Parent P9:2 was a malformed text-plus-action block, both reported as not admissible. The Candidate's faster val:0009 success (6 steps vs the Parent's 8) reflects the Parent's two wasted initial steps (P9:2 malformed action and P9:3 inventory) rather than any demonstrated benefit of the Admissible Actions section, because the Candidate's val:0009 path was the straightforward take-clean-place sequence (Q9:2 take soapbar, Q9:4 clean at sinkbasin, Q9:6 move to toilet). This limits attribution of step-count improvements to the new section.

Under the current diff the ordinary non-desklamp exact-target rule is stated more strictly: when the exact requested noun phrase has not been observed, do not acquire, clean, cool, heat, or place a different but related object, and leave a container that holds only a non-matching object. This was not reliably followed in the current clean-butterknife-and-put-it-in-drawer pair: the exact butterknife was never observed, drawer 1 held a knife 1 and a spatula 1 (P7:2, Q7:4), and both sides manipulated the near-miss knife — the Parent took it (P7:8) and the Candidate took it (Q7:9), then cleaned it (Q7:17) and moved it (Q7:19) — with both reaching the 50-step limit. In the paired put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet task the exact soapbar was likewise absent and the nearest visible objects were candle 2, soapbottle 2 and spraybottle 2 in cabinet 2 (P8:6, Q8:7); there neither side picked up a near-miss, yet both also hit the 50-step limit. So the strengthened exact-noun-phrase wording neither reliably prevented near-miss manipulation (one clear violation) nor converted an absent-target failure into success, narrowing the earlier reading that the Candidate reliably abstains from near-miss objects.

The stricter no-substitute wording coexisted with preserved exact-target acquisition and placement when the requested object was actually reachable: in the put-some-pencil-on-desk pair both sides opened drawer 1, saw pencil 1 next to a non-matching creditcard 2, took only the pencil (P5:3, Q5:4) and placed it on desk 1; in both mug-to-sidetable pairs both sides took mug 1 from diningtable 1 and moved it to sidetable 1 (P3:2, Q3:2, P4:2, Q4:2); and in the put-a-clean-butterknife-in-drawer pair both sides took butterknife 1 from countertop 2 (P6:3, Q6:3), cleaned it and placed it in drawer 1. These pairs are among the eight current pairs in which both sides succeeded, so no degradation of ordinary exact-target retrieval was observed.

Earlier incarnations of the same no-substitute principle (inside the temperature-conditioned placement guidance of the two prior edits) were examined when the exact target was absent: in a cool-a-pan task the Parent eventually took and cooled a pot while the Candidate repeatedly saw the pot without taking or moving it; in a heat-a-mug task the Parent took and heated a cup while the Candidate left the visible cup untouched; and in a hot-mug placement task the Parent took cup 2 from the countertop and heated it while the Candidate left the visible cup untouched. All these executions still reached the step limit because the exact pan or mug was not found, so abstention saved substitution steps but produced no success. This preserves the conditional-usefulness limit: the rule can avoid ineffective near-miss manipulation, but its task-level value depends on the exact target existing in an inspectable location, and the current stronger wording does not guarantee adherence either.

The current diff rewrote the ordinary non-desklamp search step to include visible open surfaces (tables, countertops, shelves, sidetables) rather than only closed drawers/cabinets, to leave an opened receptacle that lacks the target and pick a different uninspected candidate from the current admissible list, not to re-enter a location just left or repeat a short cycle, and to prefer a receptacle type not yet tried. The response is mixed. In the clean-butterknife pair both sides cycled among drawers 1–7 (the Candidate returned to drawer 1 at Q7:12 and Q7:30 and then traversed drawers 1–5 again at Q7:45–Q7:49) and hit the 50-step limit without finding a butterknife. In the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair both sides cycled among cabinets 1–4, with the Candidate adding two receptacle types the Parent never visited — bathtubbasin 1 (Q8:3) and sinkbasin 2 (Q8:19, Q8:43, Q8:49) — and still hitting the limit. So the broader-surface/no-revisit/prefer-new-type wording was followed only in isolated instances and did not break the cycling/step-limit failure mode when the exact target was absent.

The prior round's search rewrite had added: use current and recent observations to avoid immediate cycling; do not re-examine an already-open empty receptacle or check inventory while carrying nothing; and, when the obvious cabinets/fridge have not yielded the target or the step count is already high, prefer uninspected drawers, shelves, the diningtable, or other listed receptacles and new unopened containers over known-empty locations. Its observed response was mixed: in one cool-a-bread instance the Parent cycled among the fridge, cabinets and countertops and hit the step limit without finding bread, whereas the Candidate expanded to the diningtable, took a bread there, cooled it at the fridge and placed it on countertop 1, succeeding; but in another cool-a-bread pair with an identical room and contents the Parent explored countertop 3 and took the bread there while the Candidate never went to countertop 3 and cycled among cabinets, shelves and the fridge to the limit, and in a cool-a-plate pair the Candidate reached the plate in cabinet 9 only at step 49 and exhausted the budget one step later while the Parent finished at step 38. Across that round the net task-level result was slightly lower for the Candidate (6 successes vs 7), within plausible stochastic variation. Thus the anti-cycling/step-budget language was already unreliably followed, with failures concentrated when the exact target was absent.

The current diff added a distinct Admissible Actions section requiring the Actor to verify that a navigation or manipulation command is present in the current admissible-action list before issuing it, and, when a desired navigation destination is absent but a direct action on that receptacle is listed, to use the direct action or otherwise choose a listed action that advances the task. The verify-before-issuing behavior was not reliably followed: in the put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet pair the Candidate issued 'go to cabinet 3' from cabinet 1 although it was not admissible, producing 'Nothing happens' with action_in_admissible_commands=false (Q8:39), then examined that same already-open location (Q8:40); the no-clause Parent in the same pair likewise produced inadmissible steps (an empty action at P8:12 and an unavailable 'go to cabinet 1' at P8:15). In every other current Candidate pair (the eight successes) all actions were admissible, so no positive application of the fallback branch was observed, and no current task displayed a desired-but-unavailable navigation destination being replaced by a listed direct action. Thus the evidence supports only limited adherence: one observed violation, with the substitute-direct-action branch untested.

items.text: The current search refinement—treating each individual closed container and open surface as a separate candidate, not treating a container family as exhausted after one or two empty members, leaving already-open/known-empty locations immediately, and continuing to new candidates when the same small set recurs—was associated with rescues only when the Actor actually reached an uninspected surface or family. In current val:0016 (put two books in desk), the Parent stayed among desk, shelves, drawers and sidetable and hit the 50-step limit (P6:50), whereas the Candidate reached bed1 at step33, took book1, placed it in desk, returned to bed1 for book2, and completed at step40 (Q6:33, Q6:34, Q6:36, Q6:38, Q6:40). In current val:0012 (cool tomato to microwave), the Parent cycled among fridge, countertops and cabinet before reaching countertop2 at step12 and succeeding at step18, while the Candidate reached countertop2 at step4 and succeeded in 10 (P2:12, P2:15, P2:18; Q2:4, Q2:7, Q2:10). Historical family-sweep pairs show the same conditional pattern: S1_R05/P6 hit 50 without checking countertop2, while Q6 checked countertop2 at step16, found the exact butterknife, cleaned it and placed it successfully (S1_R05/P6:50; S1_R05/Q6:16, S1_R05/Q6:19, S1_R05/Q6:21); S1_R05/P8 hit 50 after cycling cabinets, sinkbasin and countertop, while Q8 checked shelf1 at step18, found the exact soapbar, cleaned and placed it (S1_R05/P8:50; S1_R05/Q8:18, S1_R05/Q8:19, S1_R05/Q8:21, S1_R05/Q8:23). These comparisons support benefit from expanding to uninspected candidates, but each task was run once and the current edit was applied jointly with the temperature clause, so whole-task differences are not attributable to this search text alone.

The refinement did not reliably stop step-limit cycling when the exact target was not found. In current val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable), both Parent and Candidate ended at the 50-step limit; the Candidate repeatedly cycled among fridge1, countertop1, countertop2, cabinet1 and cabinet2 (Q3:12, Q3:16, Q3:33, Q3:38) and did not move to the several available uninspected cabinets or diningtable candidates, so no apple was acquired or heated. Historical S1_R05/Q7 likewise failed at 50 while cycling drawers, countertops and cabinets when no exact butterknife was present, matching S1_R05/P7's failure (S1_R05/P7:50, S1_R05/Q7:50). In S1_R05/P10/Q10 both succeeded on cool-apple-to-microwave, but the Candidate needed 46 steps versus the Parent's 38 and revisited many already-seen empty locations before reaching diningtable at Q10:40 (S1_R05/P10:32, S1_R05/P10:38; S1_R05/Q10:38, S1_R05/Q10:40, S1_R05/Q10:46). Thus the evidence supports the anti-cycling instruction only as an occasional, not reliable, response; it does not overcome search failure or prevent inefficient revisits.

On a multi-instance task, the revised search did not prevent exact-count placement when the Actor chose an open surface early: in current val:0017 (two creditcards in safe), the Candidate went directly to desk1 (Q7:1), took and placed both exact creditcards in sequence, and succeeded in 9 steps (Q7:2, Q7:5, Q7:7, Q7:9), whereas the Parent inspected drawers1-8 before reaching desk1 at step16 and succeeded in 24 steps (P7:1, P7:16, P7:20, P7:22, P7:24). This preserves evidence that broader or open-surface search can coexist with sequential two-item delivery and large step savings, but the initial observation only lists receptacles and each task was run once, so the difference may reflect strategy choice rather than this edit alone.

Successive temperature-conditioning guidance—including the current step to perform the explicit cool/heat action on the held target as soon as it is admissible, opening the appliance only when necessary and avoiding repeated insert/remove or door toggling—was followed and successful in current tasks after the exact target was acquired. In val:0014 (heat tomato to fridge), Parent P4 inserted the tomato, repeatedly closed/reopened the microwave, took it out, heated it, and placed it in 39 steps (P4:6, P4:19, P4:39), while Candidate Q4 heated the held tomato at the closed microwave at step6 and completed in 8 steps (Q4:5, Q4:8). In val:0015, Parent P5 opened the microwave before heating and finished in 8 steps (P5:4, P5:5), while Candidate Q5 heated the held tomato at the closed microwave and finished in 7 (Q5:4, Q5:7). In val:0011, Candidate Q1 cooled the plate with the closed fridge at step7 and succeeded, although it took 9 steps versus Parent's 8 because it first opened cabinet1 (Q1:2, Q1:7, Q1:9; P1:5, P1:6, P1:8). In val:0012, both used direct cool actions on the held tomato at the open fridge, and Candidate's 10-step success versus Parent's 18 was mainly a search difference (Q2:7, Q2:10; P2:15, P2:18). Earlier paired cases with the target acquired showed the same direction: cool pot 18 vs 11 steps with P opening the fridge and Q cooling at the closed fridge (S1_R03/P7:15, P7:16, P7:18; S1_R03/Q7:9, Q7:11), hot apple 35 vs 9 with P inserting/toggling and Q heating held at the closed microwave (S1_R03/P8:19, P8:20, P8:33, P8:35; S1_R03/Q8:7, Q8:9), heat egg 40 vs 15 (S1_R03/P9:24, P9:37, P9:40; S1_R03/Q9:13, Q9:15), hot potato 14 vs 7 (S1_R04/P3:8, P3:12, P3:14; S1_R04/Q3:5, Q3:7), and heat tomato 21 vs 7 (S1_R04/P4:6, P4:19, P4:21; S1_R04/Q4:5, Q4:7). This supports reduced appliance manipulation and step savings conditional on locating the exact target, not a guarantee of whole-task savings when search differs.

The temperature guidance had no opportunity to help when the exact target was not acquired, and it does not repair search failures. In current val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable), both executions hit the 50-step limit without an apple or any heat action, despite available cabinets and diningtable candidates (P3:50, Q3:50; Q3:12, Q3:16). In the historical S1_R04 heat-plate pair, Parent found the plate on countertop3, heated it and succeeded in 13 steps (S1_R04/P2:4, P2:11, P2:13), while Candidate never reached countertop3, hit the 50-step limit and never had a temperature opportunity (S1_R04/Q2:50). In the historical S1_R04 hot-mug pair the exact mug was not acquired; Parent took a cup near-match at P1:28 and both eventually hit 50 (S1_R04/P1:50; S1_R04/Q1:50), while in the S1_R03 heat-mug pair both hit 50 with no exact mug acquired and the Candidate did not substitute a cup (S1_R03/P10:50; S1_R03/Q10:36, Q10:50). These cases show the guidance is conditional on exact-target discovery and say nothing supportive about success when the target is absent or unlocated.

The general non-desklamp procedure has repeatedly carried temperature-conditioning guidance, and the current edit re-added it to the acquire step: after acquiring the exact target, bring it to the appropriate appliance and perform the explicit "heat X with microwave" or "cool X with fridge" action on the held target as soon as it is admissible, even before opening the appliance; one such action suffices; do not insert/remove the target or toggle the door; then go straight to the destination. In the current pairs where the exact target was located, the Candidate applied the action on the held object at the appliance and avoided the Parent's insertion/door-toggling: in val:0014 (heat tomato to fridge) the Candidate heated the held tomato at the closed microwave (Q4:6) and placed it in 8 steps, while the Parent moved the tomato into the microwave, ran repeated close/open cycles, took it out, and only then heated it for 39 steps (P4:7, P4:36); in val:0015 the Candidate heated the held tomato at the closed microwave (Q5:4) in 7 steps vs the Parent's 8-step open-then-heat (P5:4, P5:5); in val:0011 the Candidate cooled the held plate at the closed fridge (Q1:7) whereas the Parent opened the fridge first (P1:5). The same direct-hold pattern appeared when the guidance was introduced across S1_R03 (cooling a pot at the fridge, heating an apple or egg while holding) and S1_R04 (heating a potato and a tomato while holding), with the Parent instead inserting objects and cycling doors.

This temperature guidance is conditional on locating the exact target and gave no observed benefit when the target was not found: in val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable) both the Parent and the Candidate searched cabinets, countertops, drawers and the fridge, never located an apple, and hit the 50-step limit without performing any temperature action (P3:50, Q3:50). The same limit appears in the earlier history: in a heat-plate pair the Parent found the plate on a countertop and succeeded in 13 steps while the Candidate never reached that countertop and hit the step limit (S1_R04/P2:13, S1_R04/Q2:50), and in a hot-mug pair the exact mug was not found, the Parent took and heated a cup substitute (S1_R04/P1:28, S1_R04/P1:31) while the Candidate kept searching cabinets and hit the limit without success (S1_R04/Q1:50). These instances mark cases where the clause's triggering condition (the exact target in hand at the appliance) was never reached, not evidence that the clause is ineffective.

The current edit refined the general single-pass sweep by treating each individual closed container (cabinet, drawer, fridge, microwave, safe, etc.) and each open surface as a separate candidate, not concluding a container family from one or two empty members, leaving immediately from an already-open empty or redundant receptacle, and abandoning a small set of locations that keeps reappearing without yielding the target. A coverage rescue accompanied it: in val:0016 (put two book in desk) the Parent's 50 recorded steps contain no visit to bed 1 and it hit the step limit cycling among the desk, drawers 1-4 and shelves 1-2, whereas the Candidate expanded to bed 1, took book 1, placed it in the desk, returned to bed 1 for book 2, and completed in 40 steps (Q6:33, Q6:34, Q6:38, Q6:40). In val:0012 (put a cool tomato in microwave) the Candidate reached countertop 2 and finished in 10 steps vs the Parent's 18 steps of cycling among the fridge, cabinet 1, countertop 1 and toaster before reaching countertop 2 (P2:12, Q2:4). Across the seven current pairs the Parent succeeded 5/7 and the Candidate 6/7, the difference being this val:0016 two-book rescue (each task run once). Broader per-candidate coverage can also add steps when the target is found elsewhere quickly: in val:0011 the Candidate inspected an extra empty cabinet 1 before finding the plate on countertop 2 and finished in 9 steps vs the Parent's 8 (Q1:1, Q1:2, Q1:5, P1:8).

The refinement did not overcome step-limit cycling when the target could not be found: in val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable) both the Parent and the Candidate cycled among the same cabinets, countertops, fridge and drawers and hit the 50-step limit without locating an apple (P3:30, P3:50, Q3:30, Q3:50), so the "leave immediately / stop revisiting, continue to new candidates" language did not break the loop within the budget; its benefit stayed conditional on the exact target being present at a location the sweep reaches.

The earlier single-pass family-sweep rewrite (S1_R05) was associated with two rescues where the exact target lay in a family the Parent never reached - put-a-clean-butterknife-in-drawer (the Parent hit the step limit without checking countertop2, while the Candidate found the exact butterknife there, cleaned it at the sinkbasin and placed it in drawer1) and put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet (the Parent cycled among cabinets, sinkbasin and countertop without checking shelf1, while the Candidate found the exact soapbar on shelf1, cleaned it and placed it in cabinet1) - but it did not reliably prevent cycling: in a clean-butterknife pair with no exact butterknife present both executions hit the step limit (the Parent took a knife substitute and the Candidate cycled among drawers, countertops and cabinets), and in a cool-apple pair both succeeded but the Candidate required more steps (46 vs 38). Across those ten paired tasks the Parent succeeded 7/10 and the Candidate 9/10, one trial each, and the two rescues depended on the target being present in an uninspected family; the sweep is not shown to overcome step-limit cycling when the target is absent or unlocated within the budget.

In the earlier single-pass family-sweep search edit, the Candidate found a clean butterknife on countertop2 and a clean soapbar on shelf1 after the Parent had exhausted drawers, cabinets, and the sink area without reaching those families; the Candidate thus succeeded where the Parent hit the step limit. The same version still timed out in a clean-butterknife task when no exact butterknife was found, with both sides cycling, and in a cool-apple pair both succeeded but the Candidate needed 46 steps versus the Parent's 38 while revisiting many already-seen empty locations. Across those ten pairs the Parent succeeded 7/10 and the Candidate 9/10 with no observed regression on Parent-solved tasks, but each task was run once, and the rescues depended on the exact target being present in an uninspected family.

The current follow-up diff further tightened the general search step: each individual closed container and each open surface is a separate candidate, already-open empty or matching locations should be left immediately, and a recurring small set of locations should be abandoned. Across the seven current pairs the Candidate succeeded 6/7 versus the Parent's 5/7 with no task-level success regression. In a cool-tomato-in-microwave task the Candidate avoided the Parent's repeated fridge/cabinet1/countertop1 moves and reached countertop2, succeeding in 10 steps versus 18; in a two-creditcard-to-safe task the Candidate went directly to the desk and finished in 9 steps versus 24 after the Parent opened drawers 1-8; in a two-book-to-desk task the Candidate eventually moved from repeated desk/drawer/shelf/sidetable visits to the bed and placed both books in 40 steps, while the Parent hit the 50-step limit still cycling. These outcomes are compatible with the clause enabling new-family or open-surface discovery and rescuing some prior failures, but the current diff was applied jointly with temperature guidance and each task was run once, so whole-task counts are not isolated causal estimates.

The strengthened search instruction was not reliably followed and did not prevent cycling. In one cool-plate task the Candidate opened empty cabinet1 before finding the plate, taking 9 steps versus the Parent's 8; in a heat-apple-to-diningtable pair both Parent and Candidate hit the 50-step limit while repeatedly moving among the fridge, countertop1/2, and cabinet1/2 and never reached the later cabinets, so the target was not found; in the two-book task the Candidate still revisited already-open empty drawers and shelves many times before finally going to the bed. Thus the clause can coexist with extra empty-container steps and with persistent step-limit cycling when the target is not located, and it is not a guarantee of efficient single-pass coverage.

Once the exact target was acquired, the rewritten temperature guidance was strongly associated with performing the explicit heat/cool action while holding the target at a closed appliance instead of inserting it and repeatedly toggling the door. In the current heat-tomato-to-fridge pair the Parent inserted the tomato and cycled the microwave door repeatedly before heating, succeeding in 39 steps, whereas the Candidate heated the held tomato at the closed microwave and placed it in 8; in a second heat-tomato pair the Candidate heated at the closed microwave and finished in 7 steps versus the Parent's 8 after opening the microwave. In a cool-plate pair the Candidate cooled the held plate at the closed fridge, but total steps were 9 versus the Parent's 8 because the Candidate added an empty-cabinet search visit, so the local appliance saving did not translate into a whole-task saving. Historical cool-pot, hot-apple, heat-egg, hot-potato, and heat-tomato pairs showed the same pattern of fewer appliance manipulations and steps when the exact target was found. This supports a robust local reduction in appliance manipulation conditional on acquiring the exact target, but not automatic whole-task savings when other phases differ.

The temperature guidance did not create success when the exact target was not located. In the current heat-apple-to-diningtable pair both Parent and Candidate hit the 50-step limit without an apple being found in the observed search or any heat action being performed. In a historical heat-plate pair the Parent found the plate and succeeded in 13 steps while the Candidate never reached that countertop and hit the limit; in a hot-mug pair the exact mug was not found in the observed search and both hit the limit, with the Candidate not taking or heating the visible cup substitute while the Parent took and heated a cup but still timed out. The observed benefit is therefore conditional on locating and acquiring the exact target; search failure and step-budget exhaustion remain outside what this clause resolves.
